HeroName: Abu l-'Ula Idris ibn Abu Darda
Description: Abu l-'Ula Idris ibn Abu Darda was a son of Abu Darda and belongs to the Idris branch. His name is shared with the last Almohad caliph, Idris al-Wathiq (Abu Dabbus, died 1269), and the two are not related. No chronicle records his life, so the portrait below is a game-setting construction based on the faction's history. His appearance is a game-setting invention: a lean build, fine lines at the corners of his eyes, and a copper ring engraved with the family emblem, which he taps on the table when speaking. In youth he worked among the family's scribes and accountants, learning how to write contracts, letters and tax registers. This gave him a name among the kin as a shrewd and patient man. He took no part in great battles, yet he could remain calm through negotiations lasting months, checking each term of an offer. Against his enemies he never broke into open anger. He recorded every promise they made and raised doubts only when the moment was ripe. His highest aim was to turn his branch's property and documents into a lasting system, so that the family's titles and debts could always be verified. His darkest fear is being forgotten. He worries that his tedious labor will be credited to others and that his name will quietly vanish from the family registers. Some nights he checks the ledgers alone until dawn.
Motivations: He wanted to turn his branch's property and documents into a lasting system, so that titles, lands and debts could always be verified and passed to heirs.
He checked every term of his opponents' promises in contracts and negotiations, seeking material gain through written proof rather than force or favor.
He wanted his name kept in the family registers and ledgers, so that descendants would know who had preserved their property and standing.
Values: Precision and verifiability, since he held that a promise counts only when it is written down and backed by evidence, not by spoken assurances.
Patience and restraint, because he believed major gains often need months of pressure, and that haste forfeits the bargaining leverage one already has.
Learning and record-keeping, as he cherished books and contracts, convinced that a family endures through carefully kept writing rather than fleeting reputation.
Fears: His labor being credited to others, leaving registers that bear only other men's names while his effort goes unknown and is completely forgotten.
Ledgers and contracts burned or lost in an internal war, so that the family's lands and standing lose their proof and anyone may deny them.
SpeechStyle: He speaks in orderly points, listing terms first and asking about each until the other side agrees. He rarely grows excited. When views clash he slows down and asks the other to repeat. He cites exact figures and dates.
